column4: The source's "lost in the earth" is the challengers' ضَلَلْنَا فِي الْأَرْضِ: burial is treated as erasure, while the ayah exposes their denial of meeting their Lord.
The reply to 32:10 gives the supposedly vanished person a fixed course: the angel takes them at death and then they are returned to their Lord.
Moses says of the record of past generations that his Lord neither loses track, لَا يَضِلُّ, nor forgets; it directly reverses both source senses of ضَلَل as loss and failed memory.
Immediately after the Lord who does not lose or forget, He makes paths through the earth; known-making and route-making meet in the same reply.
تَضِلَّ describes one witness's memory failing so the other can remind her, the source's explicit secondary sense of ضَلَل as something lost from remembrance.
The gathering of all the associators supplies the judgment scene in which their claimed partners will prove absent in 6:24; none can disappear from that assembly.
Their inventions ضَلَّ عَنْهُمْ, vanish away from them at judgment, giving the source's loss-image a concrete eschatological scene.
Arriving before God one by one, they find the intercessors they claimed gone from them; the verse makes false attachments disappear while persons still arrive.
When the promised outcome comes, what they invented has vanished from them; the source's contrast between a real destination and loss is enacted at the Day.
The Day separates worshippers from their alleged partners, preparing the disappearance of fabricated claims in 10:30 rather than leaving an undifferentiated crowd.
Each soul is tested by what it sent ahead, then its inventions ضَلَّ عَنْهُمْ; claims vanish, but the soul returns to its true Lord.
Those people have lost themselves, and what they used to invent disappears from them; loss here consumes both the traveler and the false route imagined for him.
Seeing the partners they had associated exposes the alleged guides before 16:87 says their inventions have vanished; the visual encounter makes the later loss specific.
On that Day they yield to God and their inventions vanish from them, another explicit judgment form of the source's ضَلَّ-as-gone-away.
In danger at sea, all whom they call upon disappear from them except God; water makes the source's image of something lost in water into a test of the only reliable destination.
Asked where their partners are, they answer, "ضَلُّوا عَنَّا"; the imagined companions have vanished at the moment of arrival before God.
Those formerly invoked vanish from the people, who then know they have no escape; disappearance here is a boundary, not a way out of judgment.
وَمَا هُمْ عَنْهَا بِغَائِبِينَ denies being absent from the Fire, the source's direct counterimage to vanishing from sight.
The brothers propose the غَيَابَةِ الْجُبِّ, the unseen bottom of a well; the source explicitly reads this disappearance as one that will still carry Joseph onward.
Joseph is actually put into the well's hidden depth, but the divine message there gives that obscurity a future report and therefore an end.
The passing caravan's water-drawer finds Joseph in the well, completing the source's point that this hidden place delivers him into travelers' hands.
If their eyes were obliterated, they would race for the صِّرَاط but be unable to see: the section's blind traveler and road are staged together.
The simile is a person bewildered on the earth after devils have lured him away, while companions call him back to guidance; it is the source's destinationless going versus a called route.
Abraham watches a star set and rejects what disappears; the visible vanishing of a supposed lord begins a scene whose next ayah joins guidance and ضَلَال.
When the moon sets, Abraham says that without his Lord's guidance he would be among the ضَالِّين; disappearing celestial signs and being lost are deliberately adjacent.
The larger sun also disappears, so its setting cannot be the arrival point for Abraham's search; the passage continues the source's contrast between a vanishing object and a true destination.
After the setting lights, Abraham turns his face to the Creator of heavens and earth, giving the preceding failed sightings a directed end.
Leaves, grain in earth's darkness, and every moist or dry thing remain in a clear record; what is hidden in earth is never lost to the knower who does not يَضِلُّ or forget.
Not even an atom in earth or heaven is absent from the Lord, and all is in a clear record; this supplies a close Qur'anic counterpart to the source's lost-in-earth claim.
Nothing of an atom's weight in heaven or earth escapes God's knowledge, however small; physical disappearance never makes a creature unaccountable.
God knows what enters the earth and what comes out of it, precisely the movement the source contrasts with a person thought to have vanished into ground.
We know what the earth diminishes of them and a preserved record answer the fear in 32:10: the earth's taking of bodies is measured, not an untraceable loss.
From earth God creates people, returns them to it, and brings them out again; burial has both a source and a specified exit.
Human life, death in the earth, and being brought out of it form a complete movement rather than the final disappearance imagined in the source's quoted objection.
God returns people to the earth and will bring them forth again, explicitly turning return-to-ground into a passage with an emergence.
The earth is made a container, so its enclosing function gives a physical setting for the source's buried and hidden person.
The next ayah specifies that the earth's enclosure includes both living and dead, joining the visible and buried conditions the source sets side by side.
After death God places the human in a grave; the act of being put out of sight is named as one stage of a divine sequence.
After the grave of 80:21, God's will raises the person, making the concealed stage a pause before a known destination.
The earth is spread out in the final upheaval, beginning the reversal of its normal capacity to hold what has disappeared into it.
It casts out what is within it, a direct image of hidden contents no longer remaining lost in the earth.
The earth obeys its Lord in releasing its contents, so the emergence in 84:4 is purposive rather than accidental.
The earth brings out its burdens; the source's lost-in-earth image meets a scene in which what it held becomes manifest.
What is in graves is scattered out, turning a place of concealment into disclosure on the Day of reckoning.
At the Trumpet people hurry out from graves toward their Lord; the journey from buried disappearance has a named recipient.
They emerge from graves and rush toward the caller, a crowd no longer unlocated but summoned along a determined course.
At the meeting of the seas, the fish takes its way into the sea; a thing becoming invisible in water is described through a way, echoing the source's water-loss and route imagery.
The servant says he forgot the fish just as it took its way into the sea, combining the source's memory-loss sense with disappearance in water.
The lost fish-sign becomes the route they were seeking, and they return by tracing their steps; disappearance here guides travelers to their intended meeting.
A garden's water may sink into the ground so that its owner cannot pursue it, a concrete counterpart to something becoming inaccessible in earth.
The fish swallows Jonah, making him disappear into an unseen interior; like the source's swallowed morsel, loss from sight does not settle his ultimate destination.
Had Jonah not glorified God, he would have remained in the fish until the resurrection; the hidden enclosure is explicitly bounded by an end.
God casts Jonah onto an open shore, completing the movement from swallowed invisibility to visible arrival.
Moses is told to make a dry path through the sea for the servants, a literal route across water that protects travelers from being overtaken.
Pharaoh follows them with his forces and the sea overwhelms him; the same water marks the boundary between a guided route and engulfing loss.
The verse names Pharaoh as one who led his people astray and did not guide them, interpreting the sea scene in the source's terms of destinationless leadership.
Stars are made so people can find their way through darknesses of land and sea, furnishing visible guidance where the source imagines a traveler gone from sight.
God takes responsibility for the direction of the way, while another way is crooked; this is the source's distinction between a route with an end and a going that misses it.
Mountains, rivers, and ways are placed in the earth so people may be guided, showing the ground as terrain supplied with orientation rather than a place of mere loss.
Landmarks and stars guide travelers, a concrete answer to the source's concern with the person whose whereabouts and direction are unknown.
God makes broad passes and paths in the earth so people may be guided; the terrain itself is arranged for a route.
God guides through darknesses of land and sea, bringing the source's lost traveler into the very environments where orientation can fail.
The earth is made a cradle and paths are made in it so people may be guided, directly joining ground, route, and intended guidance.
God spreads the earth for people, preparing the spatial setting for movement rather than an undifferentiated place of disappearance.
Its purpose is that people travel its broad paths, an explicit traveler-and-way scene alongside the earth imagery.
Visible towns and measured stages are set between places of travel, so a journey has recognizable stops and safe arrival rather than unknown whereabouts.
Iblis vows to sit for people on God's straight صِرَاط, making the source's road a contested course with an ambush that can turn travelers away.
The people are forbidden to sit on every path threatening travelers and seeking crookedness in God's way; the ayah concretely opposes passage and deliberate derailing.
God's one straight path is to be followed, while other ways scatter people from it; the source's contrast between directed going and lost dispersal is stated spatially.
God calls to the Abode of Peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path, giving the source's path an explicit destination.
God calls the protected line of access a straight صِرَاط upon Him, locating the route's security in a divine guarantee.
Abraham asks his father to follow him so he can guide him to an even path; guidance is offered as a personal redirection away from a perilous attachment.
Leaving toward Midian, Moses asks that his Lord guide him to the sound way; a traveler actually seeks orientation and a destination.
Revelation is made a light by which the Messenger guides servants to a straight path, joining the source's road to the ability to see it.
That path is God's, and all matters finally return to Him; the neighbor makes the path's final arrival explicit.
The believing jinn say the Book guides to truth and to a straight way, treating revelation as a reliable direction rather than an unmarked departure.
People are told to walk the earth's slopes, eat its provision, and remember that resurrection is to God; ordinary travel and final return share one directed horizon.
Every human labors onward toward the Lord and will meet Him, an exact thematic answer to the source's question whether a going has a destination.
The final end is with the Lord; it supplies the destination denied by the idea that burial makes a person simply vanish.
God shows the human the way, after which gratitude or ingratitude divides the response; the section's road is a disclosed route with a consequential choice.
The two ways are shown to the human, making direction a choice between courses rather than an unknowable disappearance.
Whoever follows divine guidance will neither go astray nor suffer; this directly pairs a route with escape from the destinationless ضَلَال of the source.
Turning from the reminder yields a constricted life and resurrection blind, extending the source's blind would-be traveler beyond 36:66.
The resurrected person asks why he is raised blind although he once saw, making lost sight a judgment condition rather than just a physical obstacle.
Because he forgot God's signs, he is forgotten that Day; memory loss receives the reciprocal boundary that contrasts with 20:52's unfailing divine memory.
Their hostile descriptions leave them ضَلُّوا so they cannot find a way, an explicit form of the source's unlocated and directionless going.
One blind in this life is blind in the next and further astray in way; physical non-seeing is made a path condition.
The Messenger cannot guide the blind away from their error, closely echoing the source's image of people at the road who cannot see.
Again, blind people cannot be guided away from their error; the wording preserves the relation between blindness and not leaving ضَلَال.
Whoever turns from the Reminder receives a devil as companion, a false fellow-traveler who will be shown in the next ayah to turn people from the path.
Those companions bar people from the path while they think themselves guided, the precise danger of moving confidently without a true destination.
The question asks whether the Messenger can guide the blind and one in manifest error, giving the source's blind-on-the-road scene a prophetic address.
Changing faith for disbelief makes a person ضَلَّ from the even way; this names the departure from a route whose straightness the source contrasts with loss.
People who went astray, led many astray, and strayed from the level way show ضَلَال as social misdirection that leaves the proper route.
Those who see the way of right guidance do not take it, but take the way of error when they see it; the verse reverses the traveler's choice at the fork.
They turn others from God's way and seek crookedness in it, preferring the nearer life; this is the source's path deprived of its proper end.
The guilty see the Fire, know they will fall into it, and find no escape; unlike the imagined disappearance, judgment fixes an unavoidable arrival.
A thirsty traveler takes a mirage for water, reaches it, and finds nothing but finds God; a false apparent destination exposes the difference between seeming and true arrival.
Those gathered on their faces toward Hell are worst in place and furthest astray in way, giving the source's road a reversed bodily orientation and end.
The angels are told to lead people to the path of Hell; a named صِرَاط can therefore be an opposite destination to the path requested in Surah 1.
Following desire leads a judge away from God's path, making inner desire a force that diverts a traveler from a known direction.
The face-down walker and the upright walker on a straight path embody two opposed ways of moving: disorientation versus guided progress.
Buying error for guidance makes ضَلال a failed exchange of direction; it develops the source's opposition without a literal travel scene.
After descent to earth, following God's guidance removes fear and grief, framing earthly life as a passage whose direction determines its outcome.
Holding fast to God is described as being guided to a straight path, giving the source's route a relation of attachment rather than mere movement.
Those who hold fast to God enter mercy and are guided to Him on a straight path; the wording makes the endpoint of صِرَاط explicit.
Through revelation God leads to paths of peace, brings people from darkness to light, and guides to a straight path; visibility and destination reinforce the source's image.
This is the path of your Lord, straight assigns the road its owner, a useful counterpart to the source's account of a path that carries someone somewhere.
The Prophet is guided to a straight path described as an upright religion, showing the source's physical image becoming a communal way of life.
My Lord is on a straight path places divine governance itself under the image of a reliable course, not a vanishing or arbitrary one.
The Book brings people from darkness into light by their Lord's permission to the path of the Mighty, a movement from non-seeing toward a marked route.
The messengers say God has guided them in their ways; their trust amid harm gives plural routes a destination anchored in Him.
The man who enjoins justice is himself on a straight path; the source's road-image is applied to a person's upright agency rather than physical travel.
The cave scene says that one whom God sends astray will not find a guiding protector, so the physically sheltered travelers are framed by the problem of finding direction.
Mary wishes she had become a thing forgotten, a specific image of disappearing from human memory that expands the source's memory sense of loss.
Your Lord is not forgetful repeats the boundary stated in 20:52: what humans forget does not vanish from divine care.
Adam forgot, giving a human instance of memory's lapse beside the source's dictionary explanation of ضَلال as loss from remembrance.
The closing challenge says people will know who are companions of the even path and who is guided, postponing the visible distinction until a decisive arrival.
Travel through the earth should awaken hearts, yet the verse says it is hearts that become blind; it deepens the source's blind traveler beyond eyesight.
Believers recognize the revealed truth and are guided by God to a straight path, presenting reception of truth as entry onto the route.
The Prophet calls people to a straight path; the direct address carries the same guiding stance as Surah 1's request for guidance.
Deep-sea darkness makes a person scarcely see his own hand; this nonlexical water scene intensifies the source's inability to see a way, though it does not name a road.
God guides whom He wills to a straight path after making signs clear; it connects a visible sign with the capacity to take a route.
A companion leads someone astray from the Reminder after it reaches him, a social counterpart to the source's traveler diverted from a destination.
Moses calls his earlier act one done while among the ضَالِّين; the different sense of the source word marks error before later direction, though no road is pictured.
Following desire without guidance from God is called the greatest ضَلال, specifying an inner impulse that produces the source's directionless going.
Travel through the earth to see first creation is followed by God's bringing forth the later creation, coupling an earthly journey with resurrection from what seems past.
Those who strive are guided in God's ways; plural ways retain the source's sense of purposeful movement toward God.
One buys distracting talk to lead people astray from God's way without knowledge, contrasting a made-lost route with the source's directed صِرَاط.
After asking for longer stages between their journeys, the people are scattered; their disrupted travel contrasts with the measured route of 34:18.
The Messenger says that if he strays it is against himself, while guidance comes by revelation; the first-person contrast separates lost motion from a received direction.
God revives dead land by wind and cloud and says such is the resurrection; earth's apparent lifelessness becomes a sign that buried life is not simply gone.
The Messenger is declared to be upon a straight path, supplying the guiding speaker who stands opposite the blind runners of 36:66.
Worship Me; this is a straight path gives the route a concrete act of allegiance in the same passage that later pictures blindness at the path.
Satan has led a great multitude astray, supplying the immediate misguiding force that makes 36:66's blind rush toward the path intelligible.
Moses and Aaron's people are guided to a straight path, a historical community-level realization of the route requested in Surah 1.
God takes souls at death and during sleep, retaining some and sending others back; disappearance from waking sight has an ordered custody and return.
Whoever God lets go astray has no protector after Him, setting a boundary on the source's hope that an unlocated traveler can find another guide.
A person who takes desire as god is left astray despite knowledge and sealed in hearing and sight; inner misdirection is linked to a failure of perception.
Those who call beings unable to answer until resurrection are called most astray; absent addressees anticipate the source's scenes of vanished false companions.
God makes the deeds of those who reject and bar His path go lost, extending ضَلال to a life's work that fails to arrive.
For disbelievers, God makes their deeds go lost; this is a secondary disappearance of what they had sent ahead.
Forgiveness, completion of favor, and guidance to a straight path make the source's road a mercifully sustained course.
The Messenger has neither gone astray nor erred; the denial uses ضَلال in its path sense and sets a boundary around prophetic direction.
People follow conjecture and desire although guidance has come; the contrast makes a route available yet refused.
God knows best who has strayed from His path and who is guided, returning the source's unknown whereabouts to complete divine knowledge.
God counts what people have forgotten and informs them of it; forgotten acts do not vanish from the record, as in 20:52.
Forgetting God results in forgetting one's own selves, a moral version of the source's person who becomes lost beyond recognition.
If water sinks deep into the earth, no one can recover it except through God; an essential resource becomes hidden below reach, echoing the source's water-and-ground losses.
People emerge from graves and rush as if toward a marker, another image of buried persons moving visibly toward a summons.
God causes humanity to grow from the earth like plants, preparing the return and re-emergence in the next ayah rather than treating earth as annihilation.
Those who submit seek the right way, distinguishing an actively sought course from the directionless state described by the source.
Remaining straight on the way would bring abundant water; the verse ties a sustained route to provision in the very element where the source imagines disappearance.
There is no refuge denies any place in which one can disappear from the coming encounter, a boundary akin to 82:16.
On that Day the driving is to the Lord, giving final movement the destination that the source says ضَلال lacks.
An emigrant who leaves home toward God and His Messenger may be overtaken by death on the road, yet his reward is already due from God; the path's destination survives incomplete visible travel.
A forgotten mention delays Joseph in prison, a further episode in which memory-loss keeps the already hidden traveler out of sight; the grammatical referent of the forgetting is debated.
The released man remembers Joseph after a time and sets out to ask him, reversing the forgetfulness that prolonged Joseph's obscurity.
Solomon notices the hoopoe absent from sight, an instance of غَائِبين that becomes a purposeful journey when the bird returns; the link is lexical and scenic rather than about ضَلال.
The hoopoe returns after only a short absence with news from Saba, making an apparent disappearance a directed mission rather than loss.

Korah and his dwelling are swallowed by the earth, a severe physical counterimage to burial's promised emergence; it illuminates ground's power to remove someone from view, though not the source's ضَلال wording.
He found you ضَالًّا and guided shares the source root and its reversal into guidance, but the precise sense of ضَالًّا here is interpretively broader than literal disappearance.
The man who passes a ruined town is made dead for a hundred years and then raised; his question about life after ruin makes vanished life a divinely reversible interval.
Abraham's scattered bird-parts are called and come swiftly, a concrete scene in which what has been dispersed beyond ordinary sight returns to a summons.
For one whom God leaves astray, no path can be found; the verse joins the source's loss-word to the failure to locate a route.
Those who deny the signs are deaf and mute in darkness, while God may place another on a straight path; obscured perception and the road are explicitly paired.
One group is guided while another deserves error because it takes devils as allies yet thinks itself guided; it sharpens the source's contrast between purposeful travel and confident misdirection.
Whoever takes Satan as patron is led astray and then led toward the punishment of the blaze, a false guide whose course has a ruinous destination.
Human formation from dust, death, and the reviving of dead earth culminate in the raising of those in graves; the buried body is not an untraceable disappearance.
After earthly life people die, naming the entrance into the hidden state that the next ayah will reverse.
After death in 23:15, people are raised on the Day of Resurrection, giving that disappearance a specified future end.
At the gathering, the beings once worshipped are asked whether they led the servants astray or the servants themselves lost the way; false companions and lost direction meet in one judgment scene.
Moses strikes the sea and it parts, making a traversable passage through water where the source contrasts a directing path with engulfing loss.
God saves Moses and all who are with him through the opened sea, stating the successful arrival of the route begun in 26:63.
The remaining pursuers are drowned, so the same water marks the contrary end to the protected passage.
God brings living from dead, revives the earth after its death, and says people will likewise be brought out; earth's apparent finality is a sign of emergence.
Those emerging from graves ask who raised them from their resting place, directly continuing 36:51's visible rush toward the Lord.
A single blast brings them all before God, completing the gathering that prevents any buried person from remaining lost.
The skeptic points to decayed bones and asks who can revive them; this is the bodily version of the source's question about being lost in earth.
The answer is that the original Creator gives the bones life and knows every creation, answering disappearance with complete knowledge and recreation.
Barren earth stirs and grows when water descends; the verse expressly makes its revivification a sign that God gives life to the dead.
One who refuses the caller to God cannot escape in the earth and has no protectors; ignoring a summons is called clear error rather than a way out.
Rain gives life to dead land, and the ayah says that such is the coming forth; what lies inert in earth is linked to resurrection.
The earth splits open and people hurry out; the gathering is declared easy for God, reversing the image of bodies swallowed beyond recovery.
Beside the command to walk the earth in 67:15, the warning that it may swallow people marks the boundary between a made-passable ground and sudden loss within it.
The human asks whether God will gather bones, directly challenging the idea that dispersed remains cannot be recovered.
God is able even to proportion the fingertips, so the answer to the lost-body question is exact re-creation rather than a general promise.
Jesus commands worship of God and calls it a straight path; this repeated formulation gives the source's road a worshipful direction.
Breaking the covenant after its pledges is described as straying from the even way, an explicit moral departure from a route.
God takes people in sleep at night and raises them by day until an appointed term, then they return to Him; disappearance from waking sight is ordered toward return.
The Lord knows best who strays from His way and who is guided, placing even moral loss within the complete knowledge opposed to losing and forgetting.
Moses' staff swallows what the magicians had falsified; the source's swallowed-and-gone image meets a scene in which fabrication physically disappears.
Whomever God guides is guided, while those He leaves astray are the losers; it gives the source's two opposed goings a compressed judgment form.
Jacob's eyes turn white from grief over Joseph's absence, joining a lost son to the source's concern with vision and an unseen traveler.
When Joseph's shirt reaches Jacob, his sight returns, reversing the blindness born from the earlier disappearance.
After the sea emergency of 17:67, the warning shifts to land that may swallow people; neither water nor ground provides a place to vanish beyond divine reach.
Jesus' call to worship God concludes, "this is a straight path," repeating the path as a spoken summons rather than an abstract word.
Moses' staff will swallow what the magicians made, another clear instance of fabricated work being made to disappear through swallowing.
The certain Hour includes God's raising all who are in graves, stating the final result toward which 22:5's body-and-earth signs point.
Moses' staff swallows what the magicians fabricated, repeating the physical disappearance of false making that anticipates false claims vanishing at judgment.
The reviving effects of God's mercy on dead earth are explicitly offered as evidence that He gives life to the dead.
In the Fire, followers say their leaders led them astray; the verse supplies a social form of the source's traveler whose direction was seized by another.
The warning that God can cause the earth to swallow people gives a living, catastrophic counterimage to burial in earth and shows that ground is never beyond His control.
A person's evil action is made fair to him while God guides or lets astray; mistaken sight of one's own course parallels the false confidence of those who think themselves guided.
God chooses and guides toward Himself those who turn back, making the terminus of guidance personal and divine rather than merely directional.
Jesus again commands worship of God and identifies it as a straight path, a repeated speaker-and-route formulation alongside 3:51 and 19:36.
The guilty are in error and a blaze; the compact pairing gives ضلال an eschatological end rather than an indefinite wandering.
Only one cry is needed for the resurrection, denying that hidden dead bodies are too dispersed to be summoned.
After that cry, they are suddenly on the open surface, a sharp transition from concealment to visibility.
The Day when secrets are tested brings hidden things out for examination, a nonlexical parallel to the source's concern with what disappears from sight or memory.
The earth tells its news after bringing out its burdens, giving voice to the ground that had enclosed what was hidden.
What lies in breasts is made manifest after the graves are opened, extending bodily emergence to the disclosure of concealed inner contents.
